extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legislators, political economists, reformers, and informed public interested in corporate regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the central government should recognize and regulate large inter-state corporations — choice between recognition or discrimination, limits on commission power, alternatives such as public ownership, and measures to protect both efficiency and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: substitute federal control for state control
rubrics_metrics.description: The control of the central government over commerce and the corporations should consequently be substituted for the control of the states rather than added thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State jurisdiction is partial and leads to corruption, conflicting regulation, and inefficiency; national authority should prevail because state governments cannot effectively regulate matters beyond their jurisdiction. Substitution is meant to invigorate, not enfeeble, local government.

rubrics_metrics.name: choose recognition or discrimination (no impartiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The central government in its policy toward the large corporations must adopt one of two courses. Either it must discriminate in their favor or it must discriminate against them. The third alternative—that of being what is called 'impartial'—has no real existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A policy of 'recognition tempered by regulation' favored by conservatives is effectively discrimination in favor of large corporations; policymakers must explicitly accept the implications of whichever course they choose.

rubrics_metrics.name: recognition amounts to favorable discrimination and preserves advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Any recognition of the large corporations ... amounts substantially to a discrimination in their favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition will perpetuate the corporations' existing structural advantages (capital, terminals, access to raw materials, managerial development). If recognition is adopted, the government must consider active measures to impair the efficiency of large organizations if the aim is to help small competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: repeal or revise the Sherman Anti-Trust Act if recognizing corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sherman Anti-Trust Law constitutes precisely such an attempt to save the life of the small competitor; and in case the Roosevelt-Taft policy of recognition tempered by regulation is to prevail, the first step to be taken is the repeal or the revision of that law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sherman Act signals national policy favoring small competitors; it is incompatible with a deliberate policy of federal recognition of large corporate organization and must be reconsidered if recognition is chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: consider federal incorporation act (constitutional limits noted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The thorough carrying out of a policy of recognition would demand a Federal incorporation act, under which all corporations engaged in anything but an exclusively local business would be obliged to organize; but ... such an act would be unconstitutional ... except perhaps under limitations which would make it valueless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal incorporation could create uniformity, but constitutional obstacles may render it impracticable; only expert constitutional lawyers should advise on feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: limit commission power to enforcement of statute (not managerial discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The responsibility of the legislature for the protection of the public interest is consequently delegated to a commission whose duties are partly administrative and partly either legislative or judicial ... the attempt should be to make the opportunity for good work comprehensive and commensurate with the responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute should define permissible combinations, mergers, security issues, and agreements; the commission should apply and enforce the law rather than exercise broad discretionary control over rates, service, or equipment. Use commissions as enforcement and information agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid granting commissions power to promulgate rates or control service/equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the commission is granted the power to promulgate rates, to control the service granted to the public, or to order the purchase of new equipment, it has become more than a regulative official body. It has become responsible for the business management of the corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such mixed control leads to divided responsibility, drifts into incessant and harmful interference, reduces flexibility and enterprise, favors local clamorous interests, and risks petrifying the national industrial organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: prefer bank-examiner style supervision when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps the best illustration thereof is the regulation to which the national banks are obliged to submit. In this case the bank examiners and the Controller do not interfere in the management of the bank, except when the management is violating certain conditions of safe banking—which have been carefully defined in the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where law can carefully define safe conditions, officials should only enforce those conditions; this allows private management freedom while protecting public interest. Use clear statutory standards rather than open-ended commission discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: commission as bureau of information and administrative enforcer
rubrics_metrics.description: These commissions should be constituted partly as bureaus of information and publicity, and partly as an administrative agency to secure the effective enforcement of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers should include investigating management/finance useful to Congress, receiving records of rates, and enforcing statutory definitions—functions aimed at transparency and enforcement rather than micromanagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid divided responsibility between public officials and private managers
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisive objection to government by commission as any sufficient solution of the corporation problem is the implied substitution of a system of divided for a system of concentrated responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed public/private control reduces initiative and accountability; if responsibility must be assumed, it should be comprehensive (either private with legally defined limits or fully public).

rubrics_metrics.name: preserve economic efficiency and concentration of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential condition of efficiency is always concentration of responsibility; ... in restricting it care should be taken not to destroy with the freedom the essential condition of the efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation must balance preventing abuses with preserving the concentrated responsibility that produces flexibility, enterprise, and managerial initiative—avoid measures that dismantle these conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: public ownership when corporate interest becomes essentially hostile to public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: If the interest of a corporation is so essentially hostile to the public interest as to require the sort of official supervision provided by the New York Public Service Commission Law, the logical inference therefrom is ... public ownership, if not actual public operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public ownership avoids divided responsibility; it is justified where corporate interests are irreconcilable with public welfare—but it requires administrative capacity and carries political/organizational risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: do not reduce corporate managers to tutelage under commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The great objection to the type of regulation constituted by the New York Public Service Commission Law is that it tends to deprive the peculiarly capable industrial manager of any sufficient opportunity to turn his abilities and experience to good account. It places him under the tutelage of public officials ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive tutelage undermines managerial initiative and blames are divided when failures occur. Regulation should not eliminate the manager's scope for constructive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: leave general rate-making to carriers with targeted review
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental interest of a common carrier is to develop traffic, and this interest coincides with the interest in general of the communities it serves. This interest can best be satisfied by allowing the carrier freedom in the making of its schedules—subject only to review in particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to corporate judgment on rates; provide mechanisms (courts or special tribunals) to consider specific instances of unduly high or discriminatory rates rather than centralizing rate-making authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: target illegal or unfair practices rather than structural sources of efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of such supervision is, of course, to prevent those abuses which have in the past given the larger corporation an illegal or an 'unfair' advantage over its competitors; ... The attempt to define in a comprehensive statute just what corporations may do, or must in the public interest be forbidden from doing, is not being tried, because of the apparent impossibility of providing in advance against every possible perversion ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on preventing clear abuses (rebates, unfair stock control, fraudulent franchises) while recognizing that many corporate advantages (capital, terminals, managerial skill) are structural and will not be removed by simple regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: active assistance to small competitors if fairness desired
rubrics_metrics.description: If the small competitor is to be allowed a chance of regaining his former economic importance, he must receive the active assistance of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive regulation or protection via Sherman Act is insufficient; policies aimed at leveling the field require affirmative government measures (e.g., licensing limits on size) rather than mere enforcement against abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: require recording of rate schedules and notification of special rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Common carriers should be obliged, as at present, to place on record their schedules of rates, and when a special or a new rate was made, notification should be required to the commission, together with a statement of reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency measures enable oversight without substituting managerial control; require documented justification for deviations to facilitate review and investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: empower commissions with broad investigatory powers for Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally the commission should have the completest possible power of investigating any aspect of railway and corporation management or finance the knowledge of which might be useful to Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong investigatory authority used unflinchingly would prevent mere abuses and provide the factual basis for legislative action; investigative role is central to commission usefulness when not given managerial powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid fragmented piecemeal state regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The state authorities ... began furiously to 'regulate' the railroads ... hostile and conflicting legislation which represented for the most part an honest attempt to fulfill a neglected responsibility, but whose effort on the whole merely embarrassed the operations of the roads ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piecemeal, geographically fragmented regulation creates contradictory orders, threatens system-wide operations, and can produce worse public interest outcomes than previous neglect; national-level rules are preferable for inter-state enterprises.
